subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 14 periods = 560 minutes
Total: 14 periods · 9h 20min

periods.activity_title: Spotting and naming shapes in a rangoli

tasks_in_class.description: Make Amma's rangoli on the dots given below.
Name the shapes drawn in Amma's rangoli: _____, _____, _____
How many shapes are made with (a) Curved lines (b) Straight lines
Use cut outs of shapes to make a rangoli design. Outline the object and colour.

homework.description: Try to make the following objects using shape cutouts.

time_bands.activity: Open with the rangoli picture in the book. Ask children to look carefully and name any shape they can spot. Invite a few to point to circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles in the pattern before any writing begins.
Let us Do Q1, p.44 ("Make Amma's rangoli on the dots given below.") — Children recreate the rangoli on the dot grid, connecting dots to trace each shape accurately.
Let us Do Q2, p.45 ("Name the shapes drawn in Amma's rangoli....") — Children write the shape names; discuss as a class how they decided which name belongs to each shape.
Let us Do Q3, p.45 ("How many shapes are made with (a) Curved lines (b) Straight lines") — Children sort and count, then share their counts with a partner.

Let us Do Q4, p.45 ("Use cut outs of shapes to make a rangoli design....") — Children begin arranging shape cut-outs freely; any designs started here are a creative warm-up rather than a finished product.

periods.teacher_notes: Anchor the opening to the culturally familiar rangoli image — children who have seen rangoli at home will connect quickly. A common error is calling any rounded shape a circle; nudge children to check whether the outline is perfectly round or merely curved. Additional practice with shape cut-outs (Let us Do Q5, p.45) is set as an at-home creative task.

periods.activity_title: Opening boxes to discover flat faces

tasks_in_class.description: Collect some cardboard boxes and open them up carefully. What shapes do you see in the flattened boxes?
Make an Envelope. Use a square piece of paper and fold it as shown in the picture.
Name any three objects that have rectangular faces.
Trace all the faces of any cuboidal object (example—sharpener or eraser). Answer (a)–(f) about faces, shapes, squares, and triangles.

time_bands.activity: Hold up a matchbox or cereal box and ask: 'What 3D shape is this?' Then ask what shapes children expect to find if the box were flattened. Take a few predictions.
Let us Do Q1, p.46 ("Collect some cardboard boxes and open them up carefully....") — Small groups open pre-collected boxes, lay them flat, and name every face shape they see.
Let us Do Q2, p.46 ("Make an Envelope. Use a square piece of paper and fold it....") — Children follow the folding steps; pause after each fold to notice which shape they now have.
Let us Do p.47 ("Name any three objects that have rectangular faces.") — Children brainstorm and write; pairs compare lists, checking each other's choices.
Let us Do Q1, p.48 ("Trace all the faces of any cuboidal object....") — Children trace the faces of a sharpener or eraser onto paper and answer questions (a)–(f) about what they find.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have explored circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles in the rangoli context are now meeting those same shapes as faces of a 3D object — this link between flat shapes and solid objects is the conceptual bridge of the unit. A frequent error is tracing only one face; encourage children to rotate the object and trace every distinct face, noticing that different faces may give different rectangle sizes. Ensure each group has at least one box that is clearly a cuboid (not a cube).
materials: Assorted small cardboard boxes (matchbox, chalk box, small cereal box)
Square sheets of paper for envelope folding

periods.activity_title: Building and describing rectangles on dot grids

tasks_in_class.description: Construct the rectangles using the sides given below.
Draw 3 bigger rectangles around the given rectangle.
Look at the different rectangles given below: (a) How many sides? (b) How many corners? (c) Equal sides? (d) Describe in your own words.

homework.description: Count and write the number of rectangles in the following picture.

time_bands.activity: Show children two rectangles drawn on the board — one tall and thin, one wide and short. Ask: 'Are both rectangles? How do you know?' Collect initial ideas without confirming yet.

Let us Do Q2, p.49 ("Construct the rectangles using the sides given below.") — Children connect dots on the grid to form rectangles from given side lengths, reinforcing that opposite sides must match.
Let us Do Q3, p.49 ("Draw 3 bigger rectangles around the given rectangle.") — Children draw successively larger rectangles around the starter rectangle, keeping all corners on the grid.

Let us Do Q5, p.50 ("Look at the different rectangles given below....") — Children examine a set of differently-oriented rectangles and answer (a)–(d); a short whole-class share-out surfaces the generalisation: 4 sides, 4 corners, opposite sides equal.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have traced rectangular faces from boxes now move to constructing rectangles deliberately — the shift from tracing to intentional drawing is the cognitive step of this unit. A common error is drawing opposite sides of unequal length when working freehand; using the dot grid as a constraint helps. The embedded-rectangle counting task (Let us Do Q4, p.50) is set for home practice and benefits from unhurried, systematic looking.

section_titles: Same to Same — squares vs rectangles
periods.activity_title: Matchstick squares and the all-sides-equal rule

tasks_in_class.description: How many squares do you see in this drawing? Both have ___ sides. Both have ___ corners.
Use matchsticks to make a square so that it has squares on all its sides. How many squares did you get?
Complete the squares using the sides given below.
Tick the shapes that are rectangles. Which figures are not rectangles? Explain why.

homework.description: Here is a square. Draw 2 bigger squares around this square.

time_bands.activity: Place a square and a rectangle cut-out side by side. Ask children to describe what looks the same and what looks different. Accept all answers; the goal is to surface the idea that both have 4 sides and 4 corners.
Let us Do p.51 ("How many squares do you see in this drawing? Both have ___ sides....") — Children count embedded squares in the chess/ludo-board image and fill in the comparison sentence.

Let us Do Q2, p.52 ("Use matchsticks to make a square so that it has squares on all its sides....") — An unhurried making activity: children lay matchsticks on their desks and count how many small squares appear around the border.
Let us Do Q3, p.52 ("Complete the squares using the sides given below.") — Children complete partially drawn squares on the dot grid, attending to the all-sides-equal constraint.

Let us Explore Q1, p.53 ("Tick the shapes that are rectangles. Which figures are not rectangles? Explain why.") — Children examine a mixed set of shapes and justify their ticks verbally or in writing.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have described rectangles as having opposite sides equal now meet the square as a shape where ALL sides are equal — a refinement, not a contradiction. A frequent error is insisting a square cannot be a rectangle; use the matchstick activity to show that equal sides satisfy the opposite-sides-equal property too. Drawing two bigger squares around a starter square (Let us Do Q1, p.52) is set for home practice on the dot grid.

section_titles: Same to Same — squares vs rectangles
periods.activity_title: Composing new shapes from square units

tasks_in_class.description: Use the square cutouts: How many different shapes can you make by joining (a) 2 squares (b) 3 squares (c) 4 squares. Show them in a dot grid.
Can you fold all the corners of a square sheet so that the number of corners remains the same?
Make a square on cardboard, cut along dotted lines to get 4 triangles. Make as many different shapes as possible by joining three/four triangles.

time_bands.activity: Quick recall: hold up a square cut-out and ask children to name one thing special about a square's sides. Then show two squares placed edge-to-edge and ask what shape that makes — launching the composing idea.

Let us Do Q4, p.53 ("Use the square cutouts: How many different shapes can you make....") — An unhurried making activity: children systematically join 2, then 3, then 4 square cut-outs in different arrangements and record each distinct shape on a dot grid.

Let us Explore Q2, p.53 ("Can you fold all the corners of a square sheet so that the number of corners remains the same?") — Children fold and inspect, then describe what happened to each corner and whether the count changed.

Let us Explore Q3, p.53 ("Make a square on cardboard, cut along dotted lines....") — Children cut their cardboard square into 4 triangles and rearrange them into as many distinct shapes as they can, recording outlines in their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: The composing tasks in this unit deepen the insight — built through sides-and-corners work — that shapes can be combined to create new shapes, and the same unit squares can be arranged in genuinely different configurations. A common confusion is treating a flipped or rotated version of the same arrangement as a 'new' shape; encourage children to slide and turn their cut-outs to check. The folding task is best approached as an open investigation: accept whatever children notice about the resulting shape's corners.
materials: Square cut-outs (unit size, several per child)
Cardboard squares with dotted cut lines pre-drawn

periods.activity_title: Making and testing square corners with paper strips

tasks_in_class.description: Are the corners of a square the same? Are corners of square and rectangle the same? Name objects in class that have only square corners.
Mark the square corners in these shapes.
Connect the dots to make some squares. How many different squares did you get?

time_bands.activity: Give each child two paper strips joined at a pivot. Ask them to open the strips to make a very small opening, then a very large opening, then match it exactly to the corner of their textbook. Discuss: what does 'matching exactly' feel like?

Let us Do p.54 ("Are the corners of a square the same? Are corners of square and rectangle the same?...") — Children use their strip-tester on square and rectangle cut-outs, then walk around the room naming objects that have only square corners.
Let us Do Q1, p.55 ("Mark the square corners in these shapes.") — Children use the strip-tester or a folded-paper square corner to check each shape's corners and mark those that are square.
Let us Do Q2, p.55 ("Connect the dots to make some squares....") — Children connect dots on the grid to form squares of different sizes; a quick count-round closes the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have described square and rectangle corners as 'the same' through folding now formalise that shared property as a 'square corner'. A common error is marking all corners of a pentagon or irregular shape as square corners; encourage children to test each corner individually with the strip-tester rather than assuming. Having children verbalise why a corner is or is not a square corner builds the reasoning habit the section is designed to develop.
materials: Two paper strips per child joined at one end with a brass fastener (corner-tester)

periods.activity_title: Counting and creating square corners with matchsticks

tasks_in_class.description: Look at the picture: (a) Count and write the number of corners. (b) Circle the square corners.
Use two matchsticks to make two square corners and then four square corners. Draw and show it in the space given below.
Murugan made three squares with 10 matchsticks. How many squares can you make with 12 matchsticks?

time_bands.activity: Warm-up: show a composite figure on the board (e.g. an L-shape). Ask children to predict how many corners it has and how many of those might be square corners before counting.

Let us Do Q3, p.56 ("Look at the picture: (a) Count and write the number of corners. (b) Circle the square corners.") — Children examine the figure carefully, count all corners, then circle only the square ones.

Let us Do Q4, p.56 ("Use two matchsticks to make two square corners....") — Children arrange two matchsticks to form an L (two square corners) and then four matchsticks to form a closed square (four square corners); they sketch both in their notebooks.

Let us Do Q5, p.56 ("Murugan made three squares with 10 matchsticks....") — Children work with physical matchsticks, building and adjusting arrangements to find how many squares 12 matchsticks can make, sharing their reasoning with a partner.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have tested corners with the paper-strip tool now extend that understanding to composite figures and matchstick puzzles, where square corners must be inferred rather than tested physically. The matchstick puzzle invites spatial reasoning: children often start by making three squares in a row and then see that sharing sides changes the count; encourage them to describe the pattern they notice. Allow children who finish early to try 14 or 16 matchsticks.
materials: Paper-strip corner-testers from the previous unit if children wish to check

tasks_in_class.description: Draw and name some triangular objects that you see around yourself, in your notebook.
Count the number of triangles in the given rangoli. (a) and (b)
How many different triangles can be made using the dots on this circle?
Move two matchsticks to turn the one triangle into two triangles.

time_bands.activity: Hold up a triangular flag or show the rangoli image from the chapter opener. Ask children: 'How is a triangle different from the rectangles and squares we have been working with?' Gather responses about sides and corners.

Let us Do Q1, p.57 ("Draw and name some triangular objects that you see around yourself....") — Children sketch objects from the classroom or imagination that have triangular faces, writing a name beside each drawing.
Let us Do Q2, p.57 ("Count the number of triangles in the given rangoli. (a) and (b)") — Children count systematically, circling each triangle as they go to avoid double-counting.

Let us Do Q3, p.57 ("How many different triangles can be made using the dots on this circle?") — Children draw lines between dots and record distinct triangles; pairs compare to check they have not missed any.
Let us Do Q4, p.57 ("Move two matchsticks to turn the one triangle into two triangles.") — Children work with physical matchsticks, experimenting with moves before committing to a drawing.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have been counting and naming sides and corners of rectangles and squares now apply that same analytical eye to triangles — the defining properties (3 sides, 3 corners) are confirmed rather than taught from scratch. A common error in the circle-dots task is drawing the same triangle in a different position and counting it as new; encourage children to check whether two triangles share the same three dot-points. The matchstick puzzle is deliberately open: accept any valid two-triangle arrangement.
materials: Triangular objects or pictures for the opening discussion

section_titles: Circus with circles — circle and centre
periods.activity_title: Tracing circles and folding to find the centre

tasks_in_class.description: Draw colourful circles to complete the circus scene.
Draw circles by tracing bottle caps, bangles, and rings in your notebook.
Try to make a circle on the playground.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q1, p.58 ("Name some objects that are like circles.") — Quick oral round: each child names one circular object; build a class list on the board, then ask what all these objects have in common.

Let us Do Q2, p.58 ("Draw colourful circles to complete the circus scene.") — Children use bottle caps, bangles, or the circular objects they named to trace and colour circles into the circus picture.

Let us Do Q3, p.58 ("Draw circles by tracing bottle caps, bangles, and rings in your notebook.") — Children trace several circles of different sizes; ask: 'Does every circle have a point in the middle that seems equally far from all edges?' Give each child a paper plate or paper circle to fold in half twice to find the centre point.

Let us Do p.59 ("Try to make a circle on the playground.") — Describe the activity: one child holds a rope end at the centre while a partner walks in a full loop keeping the rope taut. Back in the room, children draw and describe what happened.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have examined straight-sided shapes (rectangles, squares, triangles) now meet the circle, which has no sides or corners — this contrast is worth naming explicitly in discussion. The folding activity (fold a paper plate in half twice) is the concrete route to discovering the centre; a common misconception is that 'centre' means any interior point, so have children fold two different diameters and see that the creases always cross at the same point. Let us Do Q1, p.58 is handled as an oral warm-up and is not separately assigned.
materials: Bottle caps, bangles, and rings of various sizes
Paper plates or circular paper pieces

periods.activity_title: Comparing shape pairs and finding embedded rectangles

tasks_in_class.description: Look at these two shapes (square and triangle): discuss similarities and differences. Tick (a) corners: same/different (b) number of sides: same/different.
Choose any pair of shapes. Share the similarities and differences in these shapes with your friends.
Find the largest rectangle in these shapes.
I made one triangle, then another row. How many triangles in second figure? If one more row, how many in the third figure?

time_bands.activity: Place a square and a triangle cut-out on the desk. Ask children to silently think of one way the shapes are the same and one way they are different — then share with a neighbour before the class discussion begins.

Let us Do Q1, p.60 ("Look at these two shapes (square and triangle): discuss similarities and differences....") — Children examine the pair and tick the comparison boxes; a brief whole-class discussion draws out the idea that both have corners but different numbers of sides.

Let us Do Q2, p.60 ("Choose any pair of shapes. Share the similarities and differences....") — Pairs choose their own two shapes and prepare a short spoken comparison; a few pairs share with the class.
Let us Do Q3, p.61 ("Find the largest rectangle in these shapes.") — Children look for embedded rectangles in a composite figure and identify the largest one, justifying their choice.
Let us Do Q4, p.61 ("I made one triangle, then another row....") — Children study the growing triangle-row figure and predict the count for the third figure, writing and explaining their reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the consolidation section, which draws together the properties of all shapes studied — circles, triangles, squares, and rectangles. The comparison tasks demand that children articulate what they already know in new combinations, so resist confirming answers too quickly; let pairs disagree and re-examine. The triangle-row task is an early encounter with pattern extension: children who reason 'one row has 1, two rows have 4, so three rows have 9' are beginning to generalise — welcome that reasoning even if the exact count differs.

periods.activity_title: Torn rectangles, odd-one-out, and filling gaps

tasks_in_class.description: Here are some rectangles that are torn. How many square pieces have been torn from each shape?
Each of these shapes can be the odd one out. How is each one odd? Discuss.
To complete the rectangle, tick the appropriate shapes from the left side to fill the gaps in the shape on the right side.

time_bands.activity: Warm-up: hold up a paper rectangle and tear a small square from one corner. Ask: 'How many square pieces could I tear from this rectangle if every piece was this size?' Take predictions — this frames the reasoning task ahead.

Let us Do Q5, p.61 ("Here are some rectangles that are torn. How many square pieces have been torn from each shape?") — Children examine the torn shapes and count the missing square units; encourage them to describe their counting strategy.

Let us Do Q6, p.62 ("Each of these shapes can be the odd one out. How is each one odd? Discuss.") — Small groups examine the shape set and argue for different odd-one-out choices; a brief whole-class debate follows.

Let us Do Q7, p.62 ("To complete the rectangle, tick the appropriate shapes....") — Children select the correct piece(s) from the left to fill the gap on the right, checking their choice by mentally placing the piece.

periods.teacher_notes: The torn-rectangle and gap-filling tasks both engage the decomposition insight built across the chapter — that shapes can be broken into smaller shapes and reassembled. A common error in the odd-one-out task is stopping at the first valid reason; encourage children to find a second reason for a different choice to deepen flexibility. The gap-filling task (Q7) can be done by cut-outs if children need the concrete support.

periods.activity_title: Splitting shapes into triangles and drawing in all orientations

tasks_in_class.description: Draw two lines to split the shape into three triangles.
Draw one line to split the shape into 3 triangles.
Make the following shapes with different sizes and orientations in your notebook: (a) Triangle (b) Rectangle (c) Circle (d) Any other shape of your choice.

time_bands.activity: Draw a rectangle on the board and ask: 'Can I split this into triangles using one straight line? How many triangles do I get?' Let a child come up and draw the line, then raise the challenge: 'What if I want three triangles from a different shape?'

Let us Do Q8, p.62 ("Draw two lines to split the shape into three triangles.") — Children work on the house-shaped figure, trying different line placements; pairs compare their solutions and check that all three regions are indeed triangles.
Let us Do Q9, p.62 ("Draw one line to split the shape into 3 triangles.") — A fresh challenge with an L-shaped figure; children experiment and then explain in words why their one line works.

Let us Do Q10, p.62 ("Make the following shapes with different sizes and orientations....") — Children draw several triangles, rectangles, and circles in their notebooks in various sizes and tilts, finishing with a shape of their own choice.

periods.teacher_notes: The splitting tasks develop spatial reasoning by requiring children to visualise where a line must fall before drawing it — a different demand from the tracing and constructing tasks earlier in the chapter. A common error in Q9 is drawing a line that creates two triangles and one other polygon; prompt children to count the corners of each region. The free-drawing task (Q10) celebrates what children now know: triangles can be tilted, rectangles can be tall or wide, and circles come in many sizes.

periods.activity_title: Border designs, line patterns, and the Tangram

tasks_in_class.description: Try to make your own border designs using both curved and straight lines.
Continue the following line pattern.
Use the pieces from the tangram puzzle given in the end of the book. Can you create these shapes using some of the pieces?

time_bands.activity: Show a simple border pattern on the board (alternating curved and straight segments). Ask children: 'What comes next? How do you know?' This surfaces pattern-extension thinking before children begin their own designs.

Doors-dots-lines p.63 ("Try to make your own border designs using both curved and straight lines.") — Children design their own repeating border pattern on dot paper, using at least one curved and one straight element in the repeat unit.
Doors-dots-lines p.63 ("Continue the following line pattern.") — Children extend the given pattern in the textbook, checking that each repeat unit matches the one before it.

Tangram p.63 ("Use the pieces from the tangram puzzle....") — An unhurried making activity: children cut out or collect the tangram pieces and attempt to form the target shapes shown in the book, swapping pieces and strategies with a neighbour.

periods.teacher_notes: The border-design and tangram tasks synthesise the two strands of the chapter: identifying shape properties and composing shapes creatively. A common error in the pattern task is extending a pattern by repeating the whole sequence from the start rather than identifying the minimal repeat unit; ask children to circle one repeat unit before continuing. The tangram is deliberately open-ended — children who cannot form a target shape exactly are still engaging in spatial reasoning about how triangles and squares fit together.
materials: Tangram puzzle pieces (from the book's appendix, pre-cut)

section_titles: Same to Same — squares vs rectangles
Circus with circles — circle and centre
periods.activity_title: Whole-chapter shape gallery: connect, compare, create

time_bands.activity: Shape recall wall: children call out the name of every 2D shape studied — circle, triangle, rectangle, square — and for each one, a volunteer states one property (number of sides, corners, or something special about the sides). Scribe these on the board as a class-built reference.

Property sorting: display or draw six mixed shapes on the board (some squares, some rectangles, some triangles, some circles, one or two irregular polygons). Children work in pairs: sort shapes by a property of their choice — straight sides only, all sides equal, has a square corner, no corners — then share their sorting rule with another pair.

3D-to-2D connection: hold up a cuboid object. Ask children to name the 2D face shapes they expect to find, recall how they discovered that cuboid faces are rectangles, and identify one real object in the room whose face would be a square rather than a rectangle. Children record their answers in writing.

Create and compare: each child draws a design of their own — a rangoli, a simple picture, or a border pattern — using at least three of the four main shapes. They then label each shape in their design and write one sentence describing how two of the shapes are the same and one way they are different.

Closing reflection: children share one shape or property they found surprising or interesting during the chapter — spoken round, no writing required. The teacher accepts all responses and points back to the concrete experiences (rangoli, boxes, matchsticks, circle folding) that surfaced each idea.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws on all the concepts children have built — shape names and properties, square corners, 3D-to-2D faces, composition and decomposition — and invites them to connect those ideas across contexts they met at different points. Because the unit does not require any specific earlier activity to have been conducted, the opening recall wall is the shared foundation: whatever route children took to learn the shapes, the properties they can articulate now are the common ground. Watch for children who still conflate square and rectangle; the sorting task surfaces this and gives a natural moment to revisit the all-sides-equal distinction.
materials: Chalk or whiteboard markers for the class reference wall
Dot paper or blank paper for the design task
Shape cut-outs (available for children who want to compose physically before drawing)

items.prompt: Look at the dot grid below. Connect the dots to draw one circle, one triangle, and one square to make a small rangoli design. Label each shape you draw.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The child draws a circle (rounded closed curve), a triangle (3 straight sides, 3 corners), and a square (4 equal sides, 4 corners) on the dot grid and labels each one correctly.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify each shape by its boundary — curved for circle, three straight sides for triangle, four equal sides for square.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child use shape cut-outs to trace; stretch: ask them to add one more shape and name it.

exercise.description: Make Amma's rangoli on the dots given below.

items.prompt: Take a matchbox and look at its faces. Trace one face in the space below and write the name of the shape you traced.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The child traces a rectangular face and writes 'rectangle'; if they trace the square end, they write 'square'. Either is correct provided the name matches the traced shape.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Trace the flat face of a cuboidal object and name it by counting its sides and corners.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child use the matchbox itself to trace; stretch: ask them to trace two different faces and explain why they look different.

exercise.description: Collect some cardboard boxes and open them up carefully. What shapes do you see in the flattened boxes?

items.prompt: Priya traces one face of a brick and gets the shape shown below. What shape does she get?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Rectangle. A brick is a cuboid and its largest faces are rectangles (opposite sides equal, all four corners are square corners).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count sides and corners of the traced face: 4 sides, 4 corners, opposite sides equal — that is a rectangle.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing circle suggests the child does not yet connect flat tracing to straight-sided shapes.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing triangle suggests the child may be recalling a triangular face from a different object rather than a cuboid.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing square suggests the child knows it has 4 equal sides but does not check whether all four sides of a brick face are equal.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child trace a real box face and count sides; stretch: ask whether every face of the brick gives the same shape.

exercise.description: Trace all the faces of any cuboidal object (example—sharpener or eraser). Answer (a)–(f) about faces, shapes, squares, and triangles.

items.prompt: On the dot grid below, draw a rectangle that is 4 dots wide and 2 dots tall. Then draw a second rectangle around it that is bigger.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The child draws a rectangle with 4 dot-gaps along the top and 2 dot-gaps along the side, then draws a larger rectangle enclosing it, keeping all corners on grid dots.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Connect dots to form the required rectangle, ensuring opposite sides are equal, then expand each side outward to form the larger one.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child mark the four corners as dots first before connecting; stretch: ask them to draw a third rectangle even larger, and check that opposite sides are equal each time.

exercise.description: Construct the rectangles using the sides given below.

items.section_title: Same to Same — squares vs rectangles
items.prompt: On the dot grid below, join 3 unit squares edge-to-edge to make a shape. Draw the shape and write how many sides and corners it has.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A valid arrangement of 3 unit squares joined edge-to-edge (e.g. a 1×3 rectangle or an L-tromino). A 1×3 strip has 4 sides and 4 corners; an L-shape has 6 sides and 6 corners. Accept any correct count that matches the child's drawing.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place unit squares edge-to-edge on the grid and trace the outer boundary, then count the sides and corners of the resulting shape.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child three square cut-outs to arrange physically before drawing; stretch: ask them to find a second arrangement of 3 squares that looks different and compare side counts.

exercise.description: Use the square cutouts: How many different shapes can you make by joining (a) 2 squares (b) 3 squares (c) 4 squares. Show them in a dot grid.

items.section_title: Same to Same — squares vs rectangles
items.prompt: Cut a square piece of paper along its two diagonals to get 4 triangles. Join any 3 of these triangles to make a new shape. Draw the shape you made and name it if you can.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any shape made by joining 3 right-angled isoceles triangles edge-to-edge. Common results include a larger triangle, a rectangle, or an irregular polygon. Accept any correct drawing; shape name is a bonus.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Arrange the three triangles with edges fully touching and trace the combined outline.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child use pre-cut triangles and glue them to paper; stretch: ask whether the shape they made has any square corners.

exercise.description: Make a square on cardboard, cut along dotted lines to get 4 triangles. Make as many different shapes as possible by joining three/four triangles.

items.prompt: On the dot grid below, connect dots to draw three different squares of different sizes. Write how many squares you found.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Three squares of different sizes drawn on the dot grid, each with 4 equal sides and 4 square corners. Accept any three valid squares.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Connect equally-spaced dots to form closed shapes with 4 equal sides and 4 square corners.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: prompt the child to start with a 1×1 square (4 dots) before trying a larger one; stretch: ask them to draw a tilted square (vertices not on horizontal/vertical grid lines).

exercise.description: Connect the dots to make some squares. How many different squares did you get?

items.prompt: Arun places two matchsticks on his desk like the letter L. How many square corners has he made?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1 square corner. Two matchsticks meeting at a right angle form exactly one square corner at the meeting point.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the meeting points where the two sticks form an L — there is one, and it makes exactly one square corner.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 0 suggests the child does not recognise the L-shape as producing a right angle.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 2 suggests the child may be counting both ends of one matchstick rather than the corner formed.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 4 suggests the child is recalling the four corners of a square without applying that to a two-stick arrangement.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child physically place two matchsticks in an L and test with a paper-corner tester; stretch: ask how many square corners four matchsticks in a closed square would make.

exercise.description: Use two matchsticks to make two square corners and then four square corners. Draw and show it in the space given below.

items.prompt: Design a small border pattern using at least one curved line and one straight line in each repeat unit. Draw three repeat units of your pattern in the space below.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Three repeat units of a pattern that includes at least one curved element (e.g. a semicircle or arc) and one straight element (e.g. a line segment or angle) per unit, with the units matching each other.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the repeat unit and reproduce it consistently, using at least one curved and one straight part.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show the child a sample single unit and ask them to copy it twice; stretch: ask them to write in words what their repeat unit looks like.

exercise.description: Try to make your own border designs using both curved and straight lines.

items.prompt: Use tangram pieces to make a shape that looks like a house (a rectangle with a triangle on top). Draw the outline of your house shape and name the two shapes you used.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A drawing showing a rectangle (or square) for the body of the house and a triangle for the roof, with both shapes labelled. Accept any valid tangram-piece combination that produces this outline.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Select tangram pieces for rectangle and triangle, place them edge-to-edge, and trace the combined outline.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child arrange the physical tangram pieces before drawing; stretch: ask them to count the total number of sides in their house outline.

exercise.description: Use the pieces from the tangram puzzle given in the end of the book. Can you create these shapes using some of the pieces?

items.prompt: A rangoli has 3 circles, 2 triangles, and 4 squares. Which statement about the shapes in this rangoli is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: All the shapes are made with curved lines only.

options.label: B
options.text: More shapes are made with curved lines than with straight lines.

options.label: C
options.text: More shapes are made with straight lines than with curved lines.

options.label: D
options.text: The same number of shapes have curved lines and straight lines.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: More shapes are made with straight lines than with curved lines. Circles (3) use curved lines; triangles (2) and squares (4) together give 6 shapes with straight lines. 6 > 3, so straight-line shapes are more numerous.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Sort shapes into curved-line (circle) and straight-line (triangle, square) groups, then compare counts.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'all curved' suggests the child has not noticed that triangles and squares use straight sides.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'same number' suggests the child may have compared circle count (3) to one of the straight-line shape types rather than their total.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'more curved' suggests the child may have compared 3 circles to triangles (2) without including squares in the straight-line count.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a quick tally — curved / straight — and fill it together; stretch: ask the child to make up a new rangoli where curved and straight shapes are exactly equal in number.

exercise.description: Name the shapes drawn in Amma's rangoli: _____, _____, _____

items.prompt: Name two objects you use every day that have rectangular faces. For each object, write one thing that tells you its face is a rectangle and not a square.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any two cuboid objects (e.g. textbook, pencil box, brick, door). For each, the child should note that opposite sides are equal but not all four sides are equal — so the face is a rectangle, not a square.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the four sides: if all four are equal it is a square; if only opposite sides are equal, it is a rectangle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child measure sides of one face with a strip of paper to compare lengths; stretch: ask whether any face of the object could be a square and how they would check.

exercise.description: Name any three objects that have rectangular faces.

items.prompt: Meena draws four rectangles of different sizes and orientations. She says: 'All my rectangles have something the same.' Which of the following is the same in ALL rectangles, no matter how big or how they are turned?

options.label: B
options.text: They have 4 sides and 4 corners, and opposite sides are equal.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: They have 4 sides and 4 corners, and opposite sides are equal. This is true for every rectangle regardless of size or orientation.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check each property: count 4 sides and 4 corners, then verify that the two longer sides match each other and the two shorter sides match each other.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'all four sides equal' confuses rectangle with square — the child has not yet distinguished the two properties.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'no corners' suggests the child may be confusing rectangles with circles.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing '2 sides' suggests a fundamental miscounting of the boundary of a rectangle.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child a rectangle cut-out to fold and check opposite sides; stretch: ask which rectangles also happen to be squares and why.

exercise.description: Look at the different rectangles given below: (a) How many sides? (b) How many corners? (c) Equal sides? (d) Describe in your own words.

items.section_title: Same to Same — squares vs rectangles
items.prompt: A chess board is made of small tiles. Each tile has all 4 sides equal. What shape is each tile?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Square. A square has all 4 sides equal and 4 corners; each chess tile fits this description.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A shape with 4 equal sides and 4 corners is a square.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing triangle suggests the child is recalling a different shape and not applying the given clue (4 sides).
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing circle suggests the child is not connecting 'sides' to straight-sided shapes.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'rectangle but not a square' shows the child knows it has 4 sides but has not applied the all-sides-equal condition correctly.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child compare a square cut-out to a rectangle cut-out and check side lengths with a paper strip; stretch: ask the child to explain why every square is also a rectangle.

exercise.description: How many squares do you see in this drawing? Both have ___ sides. Both have ___ corners.

items.section_title: Same to Same — squares vs rectangles
items.prompt: Look at these four shapes: a square, a rectangle, a circle, and a triangle. Tick all the shapes that are rectangles and explain in one sentence why the others are NOT rectangles.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The square and the rectangle are both rectangles (4 sides, 4 corners, opposite sides equal; the square also has all sides equal). The circle is not a rectangle because it has no straight sides or corners. The triangle is not a rectangle because it has only 3 sides and 3 corners.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check each shape for 4 straight sides, 4 corners, and opposite sides equal — all three conditions must hold for a rectangle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: guide the child to check each shape one property at a time (sides? corners? opposite sides equal?); stretch: ask the child to draw a shape that has 4 straight sides but is NOT a rectangle.

exercise.description: Tick the shapes that are rectangles. Which figures are not rectangles? Explain why.

items.prompt: Tara folds the corner of a square piece of paper exactly in half to make a tester. She places the tester on different shapes. For which shape will ALL corners match the tester?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A rectangle. All four corners of a rectangle are square corners, so every corner will match the folded-paper tester exactly.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A rectangle has four square corners — every corner matches a right-angle tester.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing triangle suggests the child may know one type of triangle has a square corner but does not recognise that not all corners of any triangle are square corners.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing circle suggests the child has not yet understood that a circle has no corners at all.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'a shape with 5 unequal corners' suggests the child is guessing rather than applying the known property of rectangles.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child physically fold a paper corner and test it on a rectangle cut-out corner by corner; stretch: ask which other shape has all square corners (square) and why.

exercise.description: Are the corners of a square the same? Are corners of square and rectangle the same? Name objects in class that have only square corners.

items.prompt: Rajan lines up 4 matchsticks in a row to make 3 squares that share sides (like a train of squares). How many square corners are there in total in this figure?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 8 square corners. A row of 3 squares sharing sides forms a 3×1 rectangle, which has 4 outer corners. Each interior join (there are 2 of them) contributes 2 square corners (one above and one below the joining side). Total: 4 + 2×2 = 8.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw the figure, mark every corner where two sides meet at a right angle, and count them all.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child build the figure with matchsticks and use a paper-corner tester on each corner; stretch: ask how many square corners a 4-square train would have.

exercise.description: Murugan made three squares with 10 matchsticks. How many squares can you make with 12 matchsticks?

items.prompt: There are 4 dots equally spaced on a circle. How many different triangles can be made by joining any 3 of these 4 dots?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 different triangles. With 4 dots, the number of ways to choose 3 is 4 — each choice of 3 dots gives one triangle, and each is distinct because it leaves out a different dot.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List all sets of 3 dots chosen from 4: {1,2,3}, {1,2,4}, {1,3,4}, {2,3,4} — each gives one triangle, so there are 4.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child label the dots A B C D and list which three they pick each time; stretch: ask what happens if a fifth dot is added — how many triangles then?

exercise.description: How many different triangles can be made using the dots on this circle?

items.prompt: You have 3 matchsticks forming one triangle. Move exactly 2 matchsticks to turn it into two triangles. Draw the starting triangle and the ending figure in your notebook and explain what you moved.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The child draws the starting triangle, then shows two triangles sharing one side — formed by moving two matchsticks to create an additional vertex and a shared side. A valid answer: original equilateral triangle → move two sticks to form two triangles that share one side, making a total of 5 sticks used (one original stick becomes the shared side).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Move two matchsticks from the original triangle to create a new vertex opposite the shared base, forming two triangles with a common side.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child physical matchsticks to experiment before drawing; stretch: ask whether the two triangles in their final figure look the same or different and why.

exercise.description: Move two matchsticks to turn the one triangle into two triangles.

items.prompt: Look at a growing pattern of triangles: the first figure has 1 triangle, the second figure (one more row added) has 4 triangles. How many triangles will the third figure have? Write the number and explain how you found it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 9 triangles. Row 1 adds 1, row 2 adds 3, row 3 adds 5 — totals are 1, 4, 9. Alternatively, the pattern of totals is 1², 2², 3².
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each new row adds the next odd number of triangles: row 1 adds 1, row 2 adds 3, row 3 adds 5; total after 3 rows = 1+3+5 = 9.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw each row and count; stretch: ask how many triangles the fourth figure would have.

exercise.description: I made one triangle, then another row. How many triangles in second figure? If one more row, how many in the third figure?

items.prompt: A rectangle is made of unit squares. After tearing away some square pieces, the shape below remains. The original rectangle was 4 squares wide and 3 squares tall. The remaining shape has 8 unit squares. How many square pieces were torn away?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 square pieces. The original rectangle had 4 × 3 = 12 unit squares. The remaining shape has 8. So 12 − 8 = 4 squares were torn away.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply to find the original total (4 × 3 = 12), then subtract the remaining count (12 − 8 = 4).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw the 4×3 rectangle on dot paper and count all squares before subtracting; stretch: ask what fraction of the rectangle was torn away.

exercise.description: Here are some rectangles that are torn. How many square pieces have been torn from each shape?

items.prompt: Here are three shapes: a square, a triangle, and a circle. Each can be called the 'odd one out' for a different reason. Write one reason why EACH shape could be the odd one out.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Square: odd one out because it has all four sides equal (unlike triangle and circle which do not have four equal straight sides). Triangle: odd one out because it has only 3 sides and 3 corners (the fewest of any straight-sided shape shown). Circle: odd one out because it has no straight sides or corners at all.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: For each shape, identify one property it alone has (or lacks) compared with the other two.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: guide the child to list one property of each shape first, then look for which property only one shape has; stretch: ask the child to add a fourth shape and find a new odd-one-out reason.

exercise.description: Each of these shapes can be the odd one out. How is each one odd? Discuss.

items.prompt: A rangoli has 5 circles, 3 squares, and 2 triangles. How many shapes are made with straight lines only?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5. Squares (3) and triangles (2) are made with straight lines only. 3 + 2 = 5. Circles use curved lines and are not counted.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Sort shapes into curved-line (circles) and straight-line (squares and triangles) groups, then add the straight-line counts.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 2 counts only the triangles and ignores the squares.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 8 counts circles and squares (5+3) and ignores the straight/curved distinction.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 10 counts all shapes regardless of line type.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a two-column tally (curved / straight) and fill it together; stretch: ask the child to invent a rangoli where exactly half the shapes use curved lines.

exercise.description: How many shapes are made with (a) Curved lines (b) Straight lines

teacher_guide.inclusivity: [Verification failed] Refer to the book task anchored to S5.

exercise.description: Mark the square corners in these shapes.

items.prompt: A rangoli pattern has 3 rows of triangles arranged in a strip. The first row has 2 triangles, the second row has 2 triangles, and the third row has 2 triangles. How many triangles are there in the rangoli altogether?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6 triangles. Each of the 3 rows has 2 triangles; 3 × 2 = 6.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the number of triangles in each row: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw the three rows and count each triangle individually; stretch: ask how many triangles a 4-row version of the same pattern would have.

exercise.description: Count the number of triangles in the given rangoli. (a) and (b)

items.prompt: A line pattern goes: short straight line, curve, short straight line, curve, … The pattern has started with three repeat units. Draw the next two repeat units to continue it.
items.visual_stimulus: number_line: line | curve | line | curve | line | curve | ... | ...

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The child draws 'line, curve' twice more, extending the alternating pattern correctly.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the repeat unit (straight line followed by curve) and reproduce it twice in the given space.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to say the pattern aloud (line, curve, line, curve…) before drawing; stretch: ask the child to describe the pattern in words so someone else could draw it without seeing it.

exercise.description: Continue the following line pattern.

items.prompt: In your notebook, draw one triangle that is tilted (not standing upright), one rectangle that is wider than it is tall, and one circle. Label each shape.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A triangle drawn at an angle (not with a flat base), a rectangle that is clearly wider than tall, and a circle — each correctly labelled.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw each shape attending to the specified orientation or proportion, then write its name.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child trace a shape cut-out in a tilted position for the triangle; stretch: ask them to draw the same three shapes again in a different orientation or size.

exercise.description: Make the following shapes with different sizes and orientations in your notebook: (a) Triangle (b) Rectangle (c) Circle (d) Any other shape of your choice.

items.prompt: A rectangle has a gap cut into its right side. The gap is the shape of a small rectangle. Which of these pieces would fit exactly into the gap to complete the big rectangle: a triangle, a small rectangle, or a circle? Write the shape name and explain in one sentence why it fits.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A small rectangle. The gap is rectangular in shape, so only a rectangle (with 4 straight sides and 4 square corners) will fit exactly into it without leaving spaces or overlapping.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the shape of the gap (4 straight sides, square corners) to the piece that has the same boundary shape.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child cut out and physically test each shape against a drawn gap; stretch: ask what would happen if the gap were a triangle — which piece would then be needed?

exercise.description: To complete the rectangle, tick the appropriate shapes from the left side to fill the gaps in the shape on the right side.

items.prompt: A shape looks like a rectangle with a triangle on top (like a house). Draw two straight lines inside this shape so that the whole shape is split into exactly three triangles. Show your drawing.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The child draws two lines inside the house shape that divide it into 3 triangles. One valid approach: draw a vertical line from the apex of the triangle roof to the base of the rectangle, splitting the roof into 2 triangles, then draw a diagonal line across the rectangle to split it into 2 triangles — giving 4 total. A simpler valid approach: draw one diagonal of the rectangle (splits rectangle into 2 triangles) and one line from a rectangle corner to the roof apex (splits roof triangle into 2 triangles) — this gives 4 triangles; the problem says draw two lines for three triangles. Corrected valid solution: house shape is already 1 triangle (roof) + 1 rectangle (body). Draw one diagonal of the rectangle: that gives 2 triangles in the body + 1 roof triangle = 3 triangles total, using only 1 line. Two lines: draw the diagonal of the rectangle and another line — this gives 4 or more. Re-reading: Q8 specifically asks for 2 lines to split into 3 triangles for a given figure. The child should refer to the specific figure in the book; the teacher accepts any valid 2-line partition of the given shape into 3 triangular regions.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw two straight lines inside the shape so that every resulting region has exactly 3 sides and 3 corners.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child trace the shape and try cutting it with a ruler before drawing; stretch: ask whether there is another pair of lines that also gives 3 triangles.

exercise.description: Draw two lines to split the shape into three triangles.

items.prompt: An L-shaped figure is made of 3 unit squares. Draw exactly one straight line inside it so that the whole L-shape is split into exactly 3 triangles. Show your drawing and explain where you drew the line.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The child draws one diagonal line that passes through the interior of the L-shape in a way that creates three triangular regions. One valid solution: draw a diagonal from the outer top-right corner of the L to the inner bottom-left corner — this line cuts across the L-shape creating three triangular regions. The child explains which two corners the line connects.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw a diagonal from one corner of the L to another so that every region formed has 3 sides.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child a cut-out L-shape and let them fold or crease it to find a line before drawing; stretch: ask whether a different single line could also produce 3 triangles.

exercise.description: Draw one line to split the shape into 3 triangles.
